notes: Hearthvale's roads: the example set every region file follows (docs/WORLD_LIFE_ROADS.md). The Hearthvale region agent owns this file. World life, phase 1: the tithe-men off Scathe, hedge-wights at the verge after midnight, drovers and scourers and a lime-cart on the down roads, a Warden looking for her hound, the bell-thieves of Rook Wood, and the carriers between the Brow's villages. Novel round: a dove down on the road from Harewell, a scarecrow carried up to the Moot, bearers a corner short, an invitation to the wassail at night, and a gossip on a stile.

sites.notes: the Larkbourne Ford, where the Boys shake down late travellers
the ditch by the Hare and Hurdle, where the bristleback put a tusk through the lime cart's wheel
the road past Hanging Coombe, where the bell-thieves come out of Rook Wood
under Wolf Holt, on the Nauvissa road

lines.speaker: A Larkbourne Boy
lines.spring: Tell them it was the Larkbourne Boys!

name: The Scathe tithe
notes: Captain Wendle's men taking a mark a wheel on the down roads, until the captain is put down in his undercroft.

lines.speaker: A Scathe tithe-man
lines.spring: A mark a wheel, and you've no wheel, so it's a mark a leg! The captain writes everybody down!

name: The bell-thieves of Rook Wood
notes: The Larkbourne Boys' eastern gang, out of Hanging Coombe with a sack of boundary-bells.

lines.speaker: A Larkbourne Boy
lines.spring: A bell for every hawthorn! Tell them the Boys are ringing!

name: A hedge-wight at the verge
notes: A farmer buried at the hedge line who has got up to go on cutting, working along the verge after midnight. He is behind on the cutting, and you are in the row.

name: Drovers on the down road
notes: Brow drovers walking a road between folds, with news of every fold on the down.

talk.say: Morning. If you're walking the down, the fold with the lantern on the crook keeps a good fire and asks no questions. Count their ewes if you like; everybody gets a different number.

hook.rumour: The drover says {place} keeps a light for strays.

name: A lime cart off the road
notes: A Cressbourne carter with a load of quicklime and a wheel off in the ditch.

talk.say: Mind the sacks, it burns if it gets wet! -- There. That's the wheel. Hedda's lime, for the Merrowby whitewash. If you're ever at the kilns above Lime Bay, tell her I got it there dry.

name: Scourers on the road
notes: Once the Hounders have called the scouring, the Vale goes up to the Chalk Hound with rakes and pies.

talk.say: Up to the Hound! Seven years and one, and Tamsin's called us out at last. Rake the nose, rake the ear, rake the back and the tail, and all stand in the eye. Bring a pie if you're coming.

hook.rumour: The scourers are going up to {place}.

name: A Warden calling a hound
notes: A Warden of the Rest out on the down with a leash and nothing on it, while the kennel's pack is gone.

folk.name: A Warden with an empty leash

talk.say: Have you seen a hound? Big, tan, a bell on her collar? -- No. Nobody has. The whole Rest pack went over the kennel wall three nights back, and the kennel-master's sat by his gate since. Go and see him, if you're going west. He won't ask. He's too proud to ask.

hook.rumour: The Wardens' pack went over the wall at {place}.

name: A Tamwick cider pedlar
notes: A pedlar with a hand-cart of Tamwick cider and the Vale's oddments.

talk.say: Tamwick cider, pressed nineteen turns, one for every hearth on the Roll. The Mother Pippin's own, near enough. And needles. Everybody forgets needles.

name: The Brow carrier
notes: The carrier between Bramcombe and Rookdown along the Brow road: wool going east, candles and bee-wax coming west, and every piece of news on the Brow in both directions.

talk.say: Wool one way, wax the other, gossip both. Rookdown's bees have been told something they didn't like; you can hear it from the road.
Wolves on the down at night and tithe-men off Scathe by day. I earn my shilling on this road.

consequence.notice: The Brow will hear its carrier was set on.
consequence.killing_notice: The Brow carrier is dead on the road.

rescue.say: You were quick. The Brow owes you a supper, and I'll tell every fold between here and Rookdown so they know it.

name: A dove down on the road
notes: Novel round. A Fallowfold girl sat at the verge with one of the Letter-Cote's doves, come down in the road with a letter on its leg from Harewell, one of the four villages struck off the Roll Stone.

folk.name: A Fallowfold girl with a dove

talk.prompt: Ask the girl about the dove
talk.say: It came down right there, in the road, and it let me pick it up. It's one of Wenna's. Look, it's got a letter on, and it says Harewell. -- There isn't a Harewell. My gran says there was. -- Will you tell Wenna it came down? I've got to take it back but I'm scared of the cote. It's ever so tall and it all flaps.

hook.rumour: The dove that came down on the road was carrying a letter from Harewell to {place}.

name: A scarecrow going up to the Moot
notes: Novel round. A farmer walking his seven-year scarecrow up to the Scarecrow Moot on his shoulder, as the Vale does, so the farm is still said somewhere.

folk.name: A farmer with a scarecrow on his shoulder

talk.prompt: Ask the farmer where he's taking it
talk.say: Up to the Moot. Seven summers he's stood my top field, and he knows the farm's name by now, so you can't burn him, can you, that'd be asking for it. Strawe'll stand him up with the others facing home. -- Strawe's not right this summer, mind. Says he's one over. I said, one over's better than one under, and he looked at me like I'd said a terrible thing.

hook.rumour: The farmer is taking his old scarecrow up to {place}.

name: Bearers a corner short
notes: Novel round. Three bearers with a coffin set down on the verge: a coffin is carried by four in the Vale, and the fourth turned his ankle. Take the corner and they carry her on to the churchyard, and tell you where her candle is being dipped.

talk.prompt: Take a corner of the coffin
talk.say: Bless you. Four corners, she has to go on four, it's the rule, and Wat's gone over on his ankle in a rut. -- Lift on three. There. -- She was my aunt. She's having a candle dipped up at the Candle-Wheel tonight, with her name said into it, so she's not let go out. Come and see it lit if you're passing. Here, for your shoulder.

hook.rumour: The bearers' aunt is having her candle dipped at {place}.

name: An invitation to the wassail
notes: Novel round. At night, on the East Downs' roads, a merry man in old clothes stands at the verge with a wassail bowl and asks you to drink. Walk on, and he waves you off; drink, and the dancers in the ditch come up to take you to the Knap. Until the Wassail King is put down.

folk.name: A merry man with a wassail bowl

lines.speaker: A wassailer
lines.spring: Wassail! Drink and dance, and up the knap with us, and never go home!

name: A gossip on a stile
notes: Novel round. A Vale gossip sat on a stile, who will tell you something if you tell her something: gossip is a kind of prayer, the Candle says. She knows where there is a way down into the dark that you have not found.

talk.prompt: Pass the time with the gossip
talk.say: Sit down, sit down, I won't bite. Tell me something. Anything. Where've you been? -- There. Now you've been talked about, you'll keep a bit longer; that's what my mother said. My turn. I'll tell you a thing nobody in the village will: there's a way down into the dark near here that the Wardens don't write on their maps, and I know where.

hook.rumour: The gossip on the stile told you the way to {place}.
